newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK govt to appear before panel over ousted official.
newsitem.headline: HK govt to appear before panel over ousted official.

text.p: The Hong Kong government, under mounting pressure to bare facts behind the sudden departure last year of a former immigration chief, offered on Saturday to have a senior civil servant appear before an inquiry panel next week.
"Mr Lam Woon-kwong, secretary for the civil service, would be prepared to make a statement to the Select Committee as soon as practicable," a government news release said.
The news release said the inquiry committee had agreed to reconvene early next week, although no specific date was given.

The British-led administration in Hong Kong has come under intense fire to reveal reasons for the sudden retirement of Lawrence Leung, after the former immigration chief disclosed before the panel on Friday that he had been forced to leave.
Leung's testimony, made under oath, contradicted the government's earlier version that his sudden retirement was for personal reasons.

Leung, whose mysterious departure in July 1996 caused an instant uproar, was responsible for passports and immigration security, highly sensitive areas in the run-up to Hong Kong's transfer from Britain to China in mid-1997.
His disclosure took the territory by storm, dominating Saturday's newspapers, and had prominent lawmakers accusing the govenment of dishonesty and challenging it to come clean.
Terming the turn in events as Hong Kong's version of the "Watergate", newspapers in the colony demanded all the facts from Governor Chris Patten's adminstration.

"Compare what Mr Patten and others said in July with the story which emerged yesterday. It is simply not good enough for the administration to hide behind wordplay and bureaucratic procedures to leave the public in the dark," the South China Morning Post said in its editorial.

Secretary Lam told reporters on Friday that Leung decided to retire after being given a choice between retiring or waiting for Lam to make a case to Patten that his retirement would be desirable in the interest of the public.
Lam refused to say why the government had contemplated Leung's retirement and skirted questions on whether Patten had known of the matter beforehand.
Prominent politicians have also hit out at the government.
Pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau questioned testimonies senior government officials had given before the panel.
"I just don't know who to believe anymore and mind you, all these people took their oaths...and it seems now that some people are trying to mislead Legco," she said.
Legislator Allen Lee, chairman of the Liberal Party accused the government on radio of being dishonest over the affair and said the administration had a serious case to answer.
Patten, speaking from London, insisted the administration had been telling the truth and said the government would have more to say in a few days, government radio said on Saturday.
